confirmedApply.title: F12's per-hunk cost formula is duplicated verbatim between patch.ts's applier and build.ts's widening loop, instead of shared via patch-matcher.ts
confirmedApply.detail: The exact same two-line cost computation appears in both `patch.ts` (applyPatchPayload, lines ~285-286: `const patternChars = hunk.oldPat.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.length + 1, 0); const cost = lines.length * patternChars`) and `build.ts`'s `widenContext` (line 292: `const cost = lines.length * hunk.oldPat.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.length + 1, 0)`). CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §3 explains this is deliberate reuse of 'F12's fix rather than re-deriving one' — but the reuse is currently done by re-typing the formula, not by sharing code, even though both call sites already import shared T1/T3 primitives (`occurrences`, `spliceAt`, `toLines`, `Hunk`) from the exact same file, `patch-matcher.ts`, which exists specifically to hold logic 'owned by neither caller' (CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §1). A shared helper such as `patternCost(lines: readonly string[], pattern: readonly string[]): number` in `patch-matcher.ts`, called from both `patch.ts`'s work-charging loop and `build.ts`'s `widenContext`, removes the duplication with no behavior change — it is the same one-caller-then-a-second-caller extraction rationale CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §1.1 already used to justify moving `occurrences`/`spliceAt`/`toLines` there. Low risk: purely a same-value refactor, not a public API change (both current call sites are internal).

The finding survives scrutiny.

confirmedApply.title: ResolveMemo's eventsCache invalidates on trust()/untrust(), not just observe()/unobserve() as documented — false invariant in a doc comment, verified live
confirmedApply.detail:
The `ResolveMemo.eventsCache` doc comment (lines 440-450) asserts: "`applyStoreDelta` always produces a fresh `admit`/`observedById` object per `observe`/`unobserve` delta (never mutated in place), so identity comparison is exactly 'has anything been observed or unobserved since this array was built.'" This is false: `admit.ts`'s `applyDelta` (its `fromState`/`toState` helpers, admit.ts:348-370) unconditionally deep-clones `observedById` into a brand-new `Map`/`Record` on EVERY delta kind, including `trust`/`untrust`, which never touch `observedById`'s content at all. I verified this directly: `applyStoreDelta(EMPTY_STORE_STATE, {kind:'trust', pubkeys:['pk-x']}).admit.observedById === EMPTY_STORE_STATE.admit.observedById` evaluates to `false` (reference changes despite zero content change).

Consequence in `resolveRootMemoized` (store.ts:467-495): the per-root `memo.entries` cache (keyed on `chainEpoch`) correctly and cheaply short-circuits for any root already warm in the memo, since `chainEpoch` is untouched by trust/untrust (this path is what the existing SG2 test at store-property.test.ts:121-135 actually exercises — it only re-queries roots already warm in `memo.entries`, so it never reaches the `eventsCache` code path and does not catch this). But for any root resolved for the *first time* after an intervening `trust()`/`untrust()` call (a fresh memo, a new root, or simply the first `resolveRootBound` call following a trust change), the `memo.eventsCache?.observedById !== state.admit.observedById` check (store.ts:485) will spuriously fail even though the observed-event set is byte-identical, forcing a full unnecessary `Object.values(state.admit.observedById).filter(...)` materialization (store.ts:489) over the entire observed set — exactly the O(R × N) cost the memo's own doc comment says it exists to avoid, reintroduced specifically around trust changes.

This is not a wrong-output bug (resolve() still receives a content-identical events array), but it is a real, demonstrable, and previously-undocumented performance cliff triggered on the trust-mutation path this module explicitly optimizes for (D24's third epoch exists precisely so a `trustEpoch` bump stays cheap). Fix: gate the `eventsCache` rebuild on `state.observedEpoch` (which, per its own documented contract at store.ts:92/165, bumps only on `observe()`/`unobserve()` and never on `trust()`/`untrust()`) instead of `observedById` reference identity — a one-line, behavior-preserving change (same resolve() results, cheaper amortization) that doesn't touch any public surface or protocol semantics.

confirmedFlag.title: compareVersionTags loses precision on version fields wider than 2^53, silently reintroducing a digit-count ceiling
confirmedFlag.detail: parseVersionTag (line 194) does `Number(major)`/`Number(minor)`/`Number(patch)`, and compareVersionTags (line 211) subtracts those Numbers. The module's own doc comment for compareVersionTags advertises 'no fixed width and no digit-count ceiling in any field' as the entire point of the v0.7.0 amendment (F14), which retired the three-digit form specifically because it forced artificial limits (D45). But `Number()` silently loses integer precision beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1, ~16 decimal digits). Verified: `Number('9007199254740993') === Number('9007199254740992')` (both round to 9007199254740992), so `compareVersionTags('scrutiny-v9007199254740993.0.0', 'scrutiny-v9007199254740992.0.0')` returns 0 (equal) even though the two tags are textually and numerically distinct — and more subtly, two adjacent large-but-distinct values in the range above 2^53 can compare in the wrong order after rounding. This is the same class of defect F14 was written to eliminate, just moved from a fixed digit count to an IEEE-754 mantissa width. It matters because compareVersionTags feeds VER-3's implementation-vs-declared-version check in validate.ts (`compareVersionTags(single, VERSION_TAG) > 0`), so a crafted event with an oversized version field could be miscompared relative to this implementation's own version. Fix would be to parse fields as BigInt (or reject/clamp fields exceeding a documented safe width) rather than Number, and to update the doc comment's 'no digit-count ceiling' claim to match whatever is actually guaranteed.

Verified the core technical claim directly: VERSION_TAG_PATTERN is `/^scrutiny-v(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)$/` (events.ts:63, no digit-count limit), parseVersionTag (line 194-199) does `Number(major)`/`Number(minor)`/`Number(patch)`, and compareVersionTags (line 211-217) subtracts those Numbers. Confirmed in Node: `Number('9007199254740993') === Number('9007199254740992')` → true, so `compareVersionTags('scrutiny-v9007199254740993.0.0', 'scrutiny-v9007199254740992.0.0')` does return 0 for two textually and numerically distinct tags. This directly contradicts the module's own doc comment at events.ts:58-59 ("no fixed width and no digit-count ceiling in any field") and version.ts:12-15, which describe VER-1/F14's whole point as eliminating exactly this class of defect.

Checked whether this is a documented/deliberate tradeoff: searched DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md, SPEC-FEEDBACK-v0.6.0.md (F14's full text), IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md, QUALITY-AUDIT-2026-08-08.md, and the scrutiny-protocol skill for any mention of MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, BigInt, or precision limits — none exists. F14 documents the *previous* 3-digit ceiling defect and prescribes the unpadded-field fix that events.ts now implements, but never addresses IEEE-754 precision, so today's Number()-based implementation is not a reasoned, recorded acceptance of this gap — it's an oversight the amendment didn't anticipate. No prohibition on BigInt exists in the codebase or skill docs, so the proposed fix doesn't violate a stated hard invariant.

So the specific "miscompared relative to this implementation's own version" scenario the reviewer describes for VER-3 doesn't actually manifest in this codebase today. That part of the "why it matters" argument is factually shaky.

However, this doesn't refute the finding's core, category-correctness claim, which stands independently of the VER-3 narrative: compareVersionTags is a publicly exported general-purpose function (re-exported from index.ts) whose documented contract is a lossless per-field numeric comparison with no digit-count ceiling, and it demonstrably returns 0 for distinct large inputs and can misorder adjacent large values — a real, reproducible, unaddressed defect, not a documented decision, and VER-2/VER-4's explicit permissiveness toward higher/unrecognized version fields from untrusted events means large version fields are anticipated legitimate input, not an out-of-scope pathology. The fix (BigInt parsing, or documenting/enforcing a safe-width bound) is reasonable and doesn't conflict with any stated project invariant. That's a genuine, unaddressed correctness gap in a documented public contract, not a hypothetical or already-mitigated one — it just matters via general library use rather than specifically via VER-3 as framed.

This is a real, verbatim, self-authored guarantee in the module.

This is standard IEEE-754 double precision loss above 2^53-1, correctly diagnosed.

Checked for a documented/deliberate tradeoff: grepped docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md, docs/SPEC-FEEDBACK-v0.6.0.md (the full F14 entry, lines 537-626), docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md, and docs/START-SESSION-SPEC-FEEDBACK.md for MAX_SAFE_INTEGER/BigInt/precision — no mention anywhere. confirmedFlag.title: checkBinding's BD-3/4/5 endpoint typing and checkPatch's new PT-10/11 typing are coincidentally similar, not a real duplicate — leave them separate
confirmedFlag.detail:
Verdict: coincidental similarity, not worth extracting into a shared helper. Both functions share the shape "look up a referenced event, read its type, compare against an expectation, push issues on mismatch" — but every other dimension differs enough that a shared helper would need more configuration surface than the ~6 lines of duplication it would save, which is the textbook shallow-abstraction trade.

Concrete differences, read from the actual code:

1. Arity. checkBinding (lines 284-322) drives a `for` loop over a 2-element `endpoints` table (`root`/`link`), because it genuinely has two structurally identical roles. checkPatch (lines 374-395) has exactly one endpoint (`e root`) — there is no second role to justify the table/loop machinery, and adding it for a single call site would be the 'over-general abstraction used exactly once' smell this audit is explicitly watching for.

2. The type predicate shape differs, not just its value. checkBinding compares for exact equality against one `required` type per role (`observedType !== required`, root wants exactly 'product', link wants exactly 'metadata' — two different single-value comparisons carried in the `endpoints` table's `required` field). checkPatch checks set membership against two acceptable types in one branch (`rootType !== 'product' && rootType !== 'metadata'`) because a Patch's root may legitimately be *either* a Product or a Metadata. A shared predicate parameter would have to accept either a single value or a set, which is exactly the kind of parameter-shape branching that signals the two call sites don't actually want the same helper.

3. The issue-list shape per mismatch differs. A Binding typing violation always emits three issues with a role-dependent rule id: the per-role rule (`BD-3` or `BD-4`), plus the fixed `BD-5`, plus a `BD-7` *warning* for permanent caching (lines 299-309). A Patch typing violation emits exactly two issues, both fixed ids, both `error`, no warning-severity caching rule at all — deliberately, per the comment at lines 391-393 and SPEC-FEEDBACK-v0.6.0.md's F13 entry: PT-11's caching is already implied by UR-3, so no BD-7 analogue exists for Patch. A shared helper would need a variable-length, variable-severity issue list threaded in by the caller, which just re-externalizes the difference rather than hiding it.

4. checkBinding's loop interleaves an unrelated advisory check (BD-12's author-hint mismatch, lines 313-321) inside the same iteration as the typing check, with no analogue anywhere in checkPatch. confirmedFlag.title: Kind-5 (NIP-09 deletion) is a repeated hand-typed magic number across four modules, unlike SCRUTINY_KIND's single-source-of-truth treatment for kind 1
confirmedFlag.detail:
events.ts exports `export const SCRUTINY_KIND = 1` (events.ts:53) as the single named source of truth for kind 1, reused everywhere a SCRUTINY event kind is checked or filtered. No equivalent constant exists for kind 5 (NIP-09 deletion), even though it is exactly as central to the protocol (DEL-1..11) and is referenced the same number of ways: query.ts declares its own local `const DELETION_KIND = 5` (line 16) used only within this file, while admit.ts hand-types `e.kind === 5` / `x.kind === 5` at lines 180, 449, and 481, resolve.ts hand-types `target.kind === 5` / `event.kind === 5` at lines 189 and 241, and store.ts hand-types `event.kind === 5` / `target.kind === 5` at lines 212, 609, and 613 — nine occurrences of the literal `5` across four files with no shared name.

This is a real (if low-severity) duplication: the same semantic constant is spelled out independently in five places, each capable of drifting if NIP-09's kind number were ever revisited, and it is inconsistent with the precedent this same codebase already set for kind 1. It is not query.ts's bug alone — query.ts's local DELETION_KIND is actually the closest any of the five call sites comes to naming it — but query.ts is where the pattern is visible and where a reviewer would first notice the asymmetry against SCRUTINY_KIND.

Flagged for human rather than applied directly because it touches four files, at least three of which (admit.ts, resolve.ts, store.ts) are plausibly under separate audit review in this same pass and a cross-module rename risks colliding with concurrent edits.

confirmedFlag.title: widenContext / WidenResult are exported publicly, leaking an internal-only algorithm (and a patch-matcher.ts type) into build.ts's published API surface
confirmedFlag.detail: docs/CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §2.4 specifies `widenContext` as a private helper of `buildPatch` — its own pseudocode literally writes `function widenContext(...)` with no `export`, and §7 ('What this does not do') lists no new public surface at all: 'Does not add a new RuleId, HaltReason, or Severity... surfaces through the existing P4 issue, unchanged.' The actual code instead does `export function widenContext(...)` and `export interface WidenResult { ...; readonly hunks: readonly Hunk[] }` (build.ts:248, 272). Because `./build.js` is a real entry in package.json's `exports` map, every top-level `export` in build.ts becomes part of the package's public npm API — confirmed in `dist/build.d.ts`, which now declares `widenContext`/`WidenResult` and imports `type Hunk` from `./patch-matcher.js`. `patch-matcher.ts` is explicitly designed as an internal, never-published file (CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §1.1: 'the identical treatment D32 already gives ./patch... D32's internal treatment applies to it a fortiori'), yet its `Hunk` shape is now structurally reachable by any external consumer of `@scrutiny-fabric/core/build.js` through `WidenResult.hunks`. This is not required for the test suite's own use of `widenContext` — `build.test.ts` and `patch-property.test.ts` import it via a relative path (`'../src/build.js'`), which needs only a bare `export` keyword in the file, not a package.json exports-map entry; nothing forces this specific algorithm helper to be part of the *public* surface. There is also no corresponding entry in docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md or in CONTEXT-WIDENING.md §8 ('Standing decisions touched') authorizing this promotion — the only decisions recorded there are D28/D31/D11/D32, none about publicizing widenContext. Compounding this: `widenContext(before, after, startContext, ceilingWork)` takes `before`/`after` as a raw same-typed positional pair — exactly the swap hazard that motivated collapsing `buildPatch`'s own parameters into the named-fields `BuildPatchOptions` object earlier in this same file (see the doc comment on `BuildPatchOptions`: 'swapping before/after used to produce a plausible inverse patch that still passed the P4 self-check — against the wrong baseline'). Publishing `widenContext` re-exposes that exact hazard to external callers at the one new function this phase added. Recommended fix (for a human to decide, since it changes the public API): un-export `widenContext`/`WidenResult` (module-private, called only from `buildPatch`), or if external use is genuinely wanted, make that a deliberate, recorded decision and reconsider the positional before/after pair.

confirmedFlag.title: T2's out-of-range insertion clamp corrupts content when it clamps against the trailing-newline sentinel
confirmedFlag.detail:
`at = Math.min(Math.max(hunk.insertAt + shift, 0), lines.length)` clamps a pure-insertion (T2) hunk's out-of-range `@@` index against `lines.length` — the length of the `toLines` array, which includes the final `''` sentinel element that encodes the trailing-newline bit (per `lineCount`'s own doc comment in patch-matcher.ts). It should clamp against `lineCount(lines)` (already imported in this file and used two lines later at 339), the count of *real* lines excluding that sentinel.

Confirmed by executing the untracked `packages/core/test/scratch_t2.test.ts` already sitting in this working tree (left by an earlier exploration session, not written by me — I only ran it, made no edits):
- content `'a
b
'` (toLines = `['a','b','']`), in-range insertion at index 2 → correctly applies to `"a
b
X
"`.
- Same content, header index far out of range (`@@ -99,0 +100,1 @@ +X`) → clamps to `lines.length` (3) instead of `lineCount(lines)` (2), producing `"a
b

X"`: a spurious blank line is inserted before X, and the file's trailing newline is silently dropped. `status` is `'applied'`, so this wrong content is served/cached as canonical bytes — the exact RC-3 failure mode the already-fixed P3 bug (docs/AUDIT-2026-07-31.md) was about, in the same clamp expression.
- The no-trailing-newline control case (`'a
b'`) is unaffected, because there `lineCount === lines.length` and the two bounds coincide — which is exactly why this is easy to miss.

This is reachable with any T2 hunk whose header claims an insertion point beyond the content's real line count against newline-terminated content — something C6 explicitly permits producers to get wrong ('@@ line numbers are advisory'), and which `docs/AUDIT-2026-07-31.md`'s P3 section already flagged as suspicious-but-unconfirmed ('masked by the zero-clamp... the defect is real but needs a non-clamped index to observe'). The round-trip property test (`patch-property.test.ts`) never exercises it because `makePatch` never emits an out-of-range header, exactly the same blind spot documented for P3's original T2 bug. Proposed fix: change the upper clamp bound from `lines.length` to `lineCount(lines)`, and add a permanent regression case to `patch-regressions.ts` alongside the existing `t2/*` cases.

confirmedFlag.title: T2 insertion clamp uses lines.length instead of lineCount(lines), silently inserting a spurious blank line when content ends with a trailing newline
confirmedFlag.detail:
`at = Math.min(Math.max(hunk.insertAt + shift, 0), lines.length)` (patch.ts:305) clamps the T2 pure-insertion carve-out's target index to `lines.length` — the raw `toLines()` array length, which includes the synthetic trailing `''` element that `patch-matcher.ts`'s own `lineCount()` doc comment (patch-matcher.ts:38-47) explicitly says represents "the trailing-newline bit" and is "never itself a line of a diff". When the header's declared insert-after position (after adding `shift`) is at or beyond the real end of the content but the content itself is newline-terminated, clamping to `lines.length` (one past the real last line) lands the insertion *after* that sentinel element instead of before it, splicing in a spurious empty line ahead of the inserted text.

Verified by direct execution against the shipped module (content `'a
b
'`, payload with a pure-insertion hunk headered `@@ -3,0 +3,1 @@
+NEW
` — i.e. one line past the real 2-line EOF, which C6 requires to be tolerated as an advisory/out-of-range position rather than rejected):
```
result = applyPatchPayload('a
b
', '--- a/content
+++ b/content
@@ -3,0 +3,1 @@
+NEW
')
=> { status: 'applied', content: 'a
b

NEW', hunksApplied: 1, work: 0, issues: [] }
```
Expected (matching the identical scenario without a trailing newline, which the code gets right — `'a
b'` produces `'a
b
NEW'` correctly) is `'a
b
NEW
'`. Instead the canonical bytes gain an extra blank line, with `status: 'applied'`, zero issues, and no warning of any kind — exactly the "wrong canonical bytes with a status:'applied' verdict" failure class the P3 fix (commit 83d2393) was written to eliminate for `shift`, except this is the clamp on the same variable, which that fix never touched (confirmed via `git show 83d2393` — it only changed the `shift +=` line to use the new `lineCount()` helper, not this clamp). It is squarely in-scope for the module's own threat model: `patch.ts`'s own comment at this line says C6 makes an out-of-range T2 index "advisory" and deliberately clamps rather than rejects it, and `@@` line numbers are adversary-controlled on a permissionless network per RL-2's stated rationale.

Proposed fix: clamp to `lineCount(lines)` (already imported into patch.ts from patch-matcher.ts) instead of `lines.length` — i.e. `at = Math.min(Math.max(hunk.insertAt + shift, 0), lineCount(lines))`. This is a one-token change with no effect on any currently-passing case (all existing regressions either have `insertAt+shift` within range, or operate on content with no trailing newline, where `lineCount(lines) === lines.length`), and it should get a permanent regression case alongside the existing `t2/*` entries in `test/patch-regressions.ts` pinning `content: 'a
b
'` against an out-of-range/advisory T2 header, per C6.

confirmedFlag.title: Known open item 1b is half-stale: HaltRule is now in the public barrel, but the four ApplyResult variants remain unexported anywhere

Verified against the current tree, per the module-specific instruction to check finding 1b in docs/QUALITY-AUDIT-2026-08-08.md rather than restate it uncritically:

1. `HaltRule` is **already** in the barrel: `packages/core/src/index.ts:79` reads `export type { ApplyOptions, HaltReason, HaltRule, LimitKind } from './patch-types.js'` — all four type-vocabulary exports are present. This half of the finding should be marked fixed/refuted, not re-flagged as an open defect.

2. The second half is still accurate: `PatchApplied`, `PatchNoop`, `PatchHalt`, `PatchLimit` (all defined in `packages/core/src/patch.ts:44-105`) and the `ApplyResult` union (`patch.ts:105`) are exported from `patch.ts` itself but never re-exported from `index.ts`, and grepping `packages/core/src` for these four names outside `patch.ts` and test files turns up nothing — they are unreachable to a consumer.

confirmedFlag.detail: admit.ts's own top-of-file comment (lines 78-83) claims: "A malformed Binding (zero or several root/link markers, or an endpoint typed wrong) is already a BD-2/BD-10/BD-5 validity concern enforced by validate.ts before an event would ever reach this module in a real pipeline; admit does not re-derive that rejection." This is false for the actual pipeline. `bindingEndpoints()` (admit.ts:95-103) only checks that a Binding carries exactly one `e root` and one `e link` marker — it never checks that the referenced root id is actually a Product or the linked id actually a Metadata (BD-3/BD-4, surfaced as BD-5 by validate.ts's `checkBinding`, which is `error` severity: `issue('BD-5', 'error', 'Binding endpoints violate the typing rule; not admitted')`). `computeAdmission`'s Binding loop (admit.ts:198-205) and the incremental `bindingIsLive`/`activateBinding` path (admit.ts:388-399) both credit `binding:<id>` to both endpoints based only on marker-count success, trust in the Binding's own pubkey, and the Binding not being retracted -- never on validity. Meanwhile `store.ts` (packages/core/src/store.ts:318) folds every observed event into `admit`'s delta via `applyAdmitDelta` unconditionally, before and independent of computing that batch's `invalidIds` (the validity verdict is only computed afterward, in the per-event loop starting at line 326). So a Binding whose `e root` actually points at a Metadata and `e link` at a Product -- correctly flagged `invalidIds`-invalid via BD-7/BD-5 -- still credits `binding:<id>` to those two wrongly-typed endpoints in `AdmissionIndex`, and a trusted view would render them as admitted purely on the strength of an invalid Binding. `computeAdmission` (the oracle) has the identical gap, so oracle/incremental agreement (D29's cross-check) cannot catch this -- both paths share the same wrong answer. This exact gap is already documented as an open, unresolved design item in docs/VALIDATION-WIRING.md section 8 ("Design correction: a related but out-of-scope gap in admit.ts") and section 9's open question 1 ("needs its own decision before it is fixed"), written during a prior phase's design work -- but it is not listed in docs/AUDIT-2026-07-31.md nor in the current docs/QUALITY-AUDIT-2026-08-08.md findings log, so this audit round has not yet tracked it. `test/store.test.ts`'s existing BD-7 tests (`describe('BD-7 — permanent rejection once both endpoints contradict BD-3/BD-4')`) do not catch it either, because those tests never call `store.trust(...)`, so the malformed Binding never gets `direct-trust` and the credit path is never exercised -- the bug is real but currently untested in either direction. Fix requires a real decision (VALIDATION-WIRING.md §9 sketches two options: add a validity-verdict parameter to `computeAdmission`/`applyDelta`, or have `store.ts` pre-filter `bindingEvents` by validity before folding into admit's delta), which is exactly why this is being flagged rather than silently patched.

confirmedFlag.title: In-memory storage's deletion-hiding cache is invalidated by every put(), forcing a full O(total-events) rescan on the next query() even for puts unrelated to any deletion
confirmedFlag.detail:
`createInMemoryEventStorage`'s `put()` (store.ts:721-729) unconditionally sets `deletedCache = undefined` on every call, regardless of whether the batch contains a kind-5 event or an event that is the target of an already-observed kind-5. The next `query()` call with `includeDeleted` unset (the common case) then rebuilds `deletedCache` via `honouredlyDeletedIds(byId)` (store.ts:606-619, called at store.ts:732-733), which walks *every* stored event to find kind-5s and re-derive their honoured targets — an O(N) pass over the whole store, independent of how small the just-put batch was.

Phase 21's own stated goal (the doc comment at store.ts:621-635) was to replace 'one Map plus a full scan per filter' with real per-key indexes so that `query()` doesn't pay O(N) per call. For any workload that interleaves writes and reads (a relay-shaped consumer: ingest an event, then immediately serve subscribers), this deletion cache becomes the dominant cost on the very next `query()` after *every* `put()`, effectively re-imposing the O(N) scan the indexing work was meant to eliminate — the kind/tag/e-tag indexes prune candidates for the *predicate*, but the deletion-visibility filter still pays full price every time a write has occurred since the last read, whether or not that write had anything to do with deletion.

A cheaper, still-correct alternative exists without changing behavior: only invalidate/incrementally update `deletedCache` when the put batch contains a kind-5 event, or contains an event whose id is already a target of some observed kind-5 (i.e., only DEL-relevant arrivals need to touch the cache) — normal Product/Metadata/Binding/Patch traffic, which is the overwhelming majority of writes, would leave the cache untouched. I'm flagging this for a human rather than proposing the change directly because getting the incremental-invalidation condition exactly right (DEL-1 pubkey match, DEL-6 kind-5-can't-be-deleted, DEL-8 target-not-yet-observed) without silently under-invalidating (which *would* be a real correctness bug, not just a perf one) needs its own test coverage before landing, not a mechanical edit.

confirmedFlag.title: Record-key prototype hazard: an event id of "__proto__" silently corrupts AdmissionIndex/AdmitState and diverges the incremental path from the oracle
confirmedFlag.detail: toState (admit.ts:361-371) builds its plain-object views with plain assignment: `reasons[id] = [...]` and `liveBindings[id] = endpoints`; computeAdmission's oracle does the same at `out[id] = ...` (~admit.ts:214). JS semantics (verified): `o['__proto__'] = x` sets the object's prototype instead of an own property — the key vanishes from Object.keys/Object.entries, yet a property lookup still returns the inherited value. Verified end-to-end consequences: (a) immediately after the delta, `isAdmitted(toIndex(state), '__proto__')` returns TRUE because it reads the inherited array's length; (b) on the NEXT applyDelta, fromState iterates Object.entries — own keys only — so the '__proto__' event's direct-trust reason AND its liveBindings entry are silently dropped, while observedById (built via Object.fromEntries, which is __proto__-safe) keeps the event observed. resyncBinding then sees a still-observed Binding with no direct-trust and no liveBindings entry forever — the incremental state now disagrees with computeAdmission's oracle (which says the binding is trusted → live → endpoints admitted). Reachability is real: nothing in validate.ts or store.ts checks id format (grepped — no eventIdMatches/hex check anywhere before admission; ids come straight from relay-supplied JSON), so a hostile event with id "__proto__" passes V-validation and lands here. Doubly dangerous: the AG1 property gate cannot catch it because BOTH sides (toState and computeAdmission's out) use the same vulnerable representation, so they fail identically and compare equal. Fix direction: build these records with Object.fromEntries (or null-prototype objects) in both toState and computeAdmission, and/or make isAdmitted use Object.hasOwn; also worth a property-generator id that occasionally emits '__proto__'/'constructor' so the gate actually sees the shape.

This is not a coincidental resemblance — it uses the identical variable names (`marker`, `id`, `relay`) taken straight from `eTags`, and explicitly frames the conditional-spread as the required technique ("Spread conditionally instead of assigning `undefined`") for satisfying `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` when a value comes from `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`-typed tag access. This is a deliberate, documented, taught idiom for precisely this situation in this codebase — the opposite of an ad hoc duplication that "isn't an established idiom." `eTags` has two structurally identical optional fields (`marker`, `authorHint`) both sourced from indexed tag access, so applying the documented idiom twice is correct, consistent use of house style, not accidental repetition.

Given that, extracting a local `optIf` helper (as proposed) would actually deviate from the documented convention other contributors/agents are told to follow, and would add an abstraction for a two-line, self-explanatory pattern inside a single function — something the project's own "Simplicity First" guidance (no abstractions for single-use/local code) would push back on. I also checked docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md; it does not mention this specific case, but the typescript-strict skill is the more directly relevant, applicable documentation and it settles the question.

Nothing else about the finding is factually wrong (the duplication is real, tests use toEqual so the refactor wouldn't break them, no exported symbol is touched) — but "not an idiom being followed" is the load-bearing claim justifying the fix, and it's contradicted by the repo's own style documentation. That's enough to refute this as a valid audit finding: it's a stylistic nit that mischaracterizes deliberate, documented convention as an oversight worth fixing.

The finding's factual premise is wrong. It claims the `...(x !== undefined && x !== '' ? { key: x } : {})` pattern "doesn't appear anywhere else in the package, so it isn't an established codebase idiom being followed." But `.claude/skills/typescript-strict/SKILL.md` (this repo's own documented TypeScript conventions, loaded whenever anyone edits .ts files here) explicitly prescribes this exact pattern as the canonical way to satisfy `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, and its worked example is literally `return { id, relay, ...(marker !== undefined ? { marker } : {}) }` — the same `id`/`relay`/`marker` shape as `eTags`. So the two inline conditionals in `eTags` aren't an ad hoc duplication invented on the spot; they are two applications of the package's documented, mandated idiom for this exact TypeScript compiler setting, applied consistently and locally.

Given that, extracting a local helper (`optIf`) or switching to mutable if-statement construction, as the reviewer proposes, would actually deviate from the documented house style rather than align with it — it would introduce a one-off abstraction/pattern not used or sanctioned anywhere else, to save two lines in one function. That cuts directly against this project's own "no abstractions for single-use code" and "match existing style" conventions.

I confirmed via Grep that the pattern indeed appears only at these two lines in `packages/core/src` (so the "twice, inline" observation is accurate), and `docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md` has no entry on it — but the governing document isn't the decisions log here, it's the typescript-strict skill, and it settles the question: this is the prescribed idiom, not an oversight or unconsidered duplication. Severity was already flagged "low-value" by the reviewer; with the idiom now shown to be intentional and documented, there's no defect left to fix — refactoring it would fight the codebase's own strict-TypeScript guidance for no real gain.

Verified the code at packages/core/src/events.ts:105-119. The finding is factually accurate: lines 114-115 do repeat the identical `...(x !== undefined && x !== '' ? { key: x } : {})` conditional-spread shape for `marker` and `authorHint`, and a repo-wide grep confirms this exact pattern occurs nowhere else in packages/core/src (the only superficially similar snippet, in store.ts:866, is a different shape — a ternary assigned to a variable, with no empty-string check — so it isn't the same idiom being followed elsewhere). No entry in docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md documents this specific duplication as a deliberate tradeoff; grepping for exactOptionalPropertyTypes/conditional-spread/BD-8/BD-12 in that file turns up nothing.

So the finding isn't wrong about the code, and it isn't a documented deliberate decision. But it fails on a different axis: whether it's a genuine, worthwhile simplification rather than a nitpick that shouldn't be actioned. The duplication is exactly two occurrences of a one-line ternary, inside a single 8-line function, used only there. This is well below the conventional 'rule of three' threshold for extracting a helper, and the reviewer's own proposed fixes (a generic `optIf` helper, or two `if` statements building a mutable object) trade two inline, locally-obvious lines for either a new generic abstraction used at exactly two call sites in the entire package, or a shift from declarative object-literal construction to imperative mutation — neither is a clear readability or maintainability win. The pattern exists to satisfy exactOptionalPropertyTypes while implementing the documented BD-8/BD-12 empty-string-means-absent semantics, and is transparent as written. refuted.title: T1's uniqueness count ignores the oldNoEol marker, causing a spurious ambiguous-match halt where the module's own design doc says the marker should disambiguate
refuted.detail:
`occurrences(lines, hunk.oldPat)` at line 311 counts every textual occurrence of the pattern with no regard to `hunk.oldNoEol`; the EOF-consistency check (`spliceAt`'s case-A/B branches in patch-matcher.ts:174-201) only runs afterward, against whichever single match T1 already picked. If the same pattern occurs twice — once at the true end of content (consistent with `oldNoEol`) and once mid-file (inconsistent with it) — `occurrences` reports `count === 2` and the hunk HALTs as `ambiguous-match` before the EOF marker is ever consulted, even though only one of the two textual matches is actually a valid position for this hunk.

Confirmed by executing the untracked `packages/core/test/zz-verify-bug.test.ts` already present in this working tree (again, I only ran it, made no edits): content `'x
DUP1
DUP2
y
DUP1
DUP2'` (no trailing newline) with a hunk whose old side is `DUP1
DUP2` marked `\ No newline at end of file` halts with `ambiguous-match`, even though the mid-file occurrence (at line 2) cannot possibly be what the hunk means — it isn't the end of the file, and the hunk explicitly asserts it is.

Whether the correct fix is to filter candidate positions by EOF-consistency before counting (so the case above applies cleanly) or whether a strict textual reading of T1 ('the pattern MUST occur exactly once') really does mandate treating this as ambiguous regardless of EOF markers, is a judgment call — the spec doesn't address this composition explicitly, so it may warrant a SPEC-FEEDBACK entry (like F6/F12 elsewhere in this same file) rather than a silent behavior change. refuted.title: pendingAwaiting leaks a stale entry when a Binding's two awaited endpoints resolve asymmetrically (one triggers 'invalid', the other's registration is never cleared)
refuted.detail:
store.ts's own comment at lines 264-265 claims: 'a still-unresolved awaited id from an earlier partial check is re-derived, not pruned, by the re-validation below.' This is false for a Binding awaiting BOTH endpoints (BD-6) when one endpoint's arrival makes the other endpoint's typing check produce a terminal 'invalid' verdict while the other endpoint is still unobserved.

Mechanism: validate.ts's checkBinding (lines 258-333) loops over BOTH endpoints unconditionally (`for (const { ref, role, required, rule } of endpoints)`, no early return), so it can simultaneously push an error issue for one endpoint (wrong type -> BD-3/BD-4 + BD-5 'error') AND push the other, still-unobserved endpoint's id onto `awaiting` in the same call. But validateEvent (lines 101-107) checks `hasError(issues)` BEFORE checking `awaiting.length`, so once any error is present it returns `{status: 'invalid', issues}` -- a variant that carries no `awaiting` field at all. The populated `awaiting` array is silently discarded.

Back in store.ts, `applyVerdict` (lines 157-169) only ever ADDS entries to `pendingAwaiting` when `verdict.status === 'pending'`; on an 'invalid' verdict it does nothing beyond `invalidIds.add(event.id)`. The caller loop that triggered the re-check (lines 260-281) only removes the ONE awaited-id entry that just arrived (`removeAwaiting(pendingAwaiting, event.id, pendingId)`), never any of the event's OTHER still-registered awaited-id entries.

Concrete repro: Binding B has `e root` -> X (unobserved) and `e link` -> L (unobserved). `add([B])`: verdict is pending, awaiting=[X, L]; pendingAwaiting[X]={B}, pendingAwaiting[L]={B}. Now `add([X])` where X turns out to be a Patch, not a Product (wrong type for the root role): processObservedEvent(X) finds pendingAwaiting[X]={B}, removes that one entry, then re-validates B. checkBinding now sees root=X (wrong type, pushes BD-3/BD-5 error) and continues to link=L (still unobserved, pushes L onto awaiting) -- but hasError wins, so validateEvent returns 'invalid' and the awaiting=[L] is thrown away. store correctly adds B to invalidIds, but pendingAwaiting[L]={B} is NEVER cleaned up. If L never arrives, this entry sits in `StoreState.pendingAwaiting` forever (unbounded growth for a long-running store). Even explicitly `unobserve([B])` doesn't clean it: the unobserve cleanup path (lines 370-375) only fires `if (verdict.status === 'pending')`, and re-validating the already-terminally-invalid B returns 'invalid', not 'pending', so the stale pendingAwaiting[L] entry survives B's own removal too.

This is a genuine, previously-unreported gap (not the same as the already-fixed P6/P5 items or the documented arrival-order-dependent chainEpoch quirk). It's also structurally invisible to the existing SG1 confluence gate: `toStoreView` (STORE.md §9) deliberately excludes `pendingAwaiting` from the compared projection (for legitimate, unrelated reasons -- arrival-order-dependent cache bookkeeping), so no existing property test can catch this leak even if the fuzzer happened to generate the triggering interleaving. All existing BD-7 tests in store.test.ts either deliver both endpoints in one batched add() call (never reaching the asymmetric partial-await case, since admitAfter.observedById already contains every batch member before checkBinding runs) or don't probe pendingAwaiting content after an asymmetric-arrival BD-7 rejection.

Suggested fix direction (for a human to design, not one-line): either (a) have checkBinding short-circuit and stop appending to `awaiting` once an error is pushed for an already-checked endpoint (mirroring checkPatch's own return-immediately-after-awaiting discipline at validate.ts:378-379/404-405), so `awaiting` and error issues are never populated together in the same verdict, or (b) have store.ts's applyVerdict, on a fresh 'invalid' verdict, proactively scrub the event's id out of every pendingAwaiting bucket it might still be registered under (requires either a reverse id->awaited-ids index or an accepted O(pendingAwaiting) scan).

refuted.title: cascade() is O(patches × depth): each fixpoint round rescans every candidate
refuted.detail: The `for (let changed = true; changed;)` loop re-scans all `candidates` once per propagation round, so a deleted first patch in a depth-D chain costs D rounds × N candidates = O(N·D). Realistic depth is ≤1 (AUDIT-2026-07-31 §4), but resolve() accepts an arbitrary observed set and no §5.4 ceiling bounds chain length — an adversarial corpus of ~10k chained patches turns deletion handling into ~10^8 set lookups per resolve call. A children-index BFS from the directly-deleted candidates (build parent→children map once, walk it) is O(N) and yields the identical set: the operator is monotone so the fixpoint is unique, and `removed` is only ever membership-tested, so no observable behavior changes. Same for the walk's existing children map — it could be shared with cascade instead of building the parent relation twice.
